newsitem.title: USA: Data show U.S. work force not as mobile as thought.
newsitem.headline: Data show U.S. work force not as mobile as thought.

text.p: Men have been changing jobs more frequently in recent years but women have generally defied the widely held belief that the American work force has become increasingly mobile, the government said Thursday.

Indeed, female workers surveyed in 1996 said they have been with their current employers for even longer periods than those surveyed five years ago, according to data released by the Bureau of Labour Statistics. In contrast, median tenure among men has fallen in nearly every age group.

Median tenure -- the point at which half the workers had more tenure and half had less -- among men has been on the wane since 1983 in nearly all age groups, with the biggest drops occurring among men between the ages of 45 and 64, the government said.

For men 25 years and older, median tenure was at 5.3 years in 1996, 5.4 years in 1991, 5.7 years in 1987 and 5.9 years in 1983. For females, tenure was at 4.7 years in 1996, 4.3 years in both 1991 and 1987, and at 4.2 years in 1983.
The Labour Department report noted difficulties in trying to interpret a change in tenure trends as a sign of either worsening or improving job security.
In an economic boom, for example, more jobs become available for new entrants to the work force, which could cause a drop in median tenure levels as the proportion of longer-term workers declines.
"There's nothing inherently good or bad about long tenure or short tenure," said Jay Meisenheimer, a BLS economist. "There are a lot of people who are voluntarily moving."
For women, however, the data showing them staying put longer likely reflect the relatively recent success women have had in gaining higher-level jobs.

"You're seeing more and more females in the labour force as professionals," said Paul Yakoboski, a researcher at the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a public policy group that recently released a study on tenure trends.
The data on men tends to confirm the theory that young workers no longer expect to join companies early in their careers and stay with them for life, Yakoboski said.
What's more, he said, corporate restructurings and widespread layoffs have played a key role in the increased mobility of men in the workplace.
But others minimised the impact of corporate downsizing on job tenure statistics.

"There's been a lot of discussion about increased insecurity among American workers," said Henry Farber, professor of economics at Princeton University. "There has not been dramatic change in the structure of employment despite all the publicity about (layoffs)."
Farber, who has tracked the data closely over the years, described current patterns in the tenure data as consistent with trends of recent years.
